title: Chonyo, the Second Son of Shimon HaTzaddik
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.
copyright: English translation and editorial notes © 2026 Joshua Waxman. All rights reserved.
paragraphs: Menachot 109b relates that Shimon HaTzaddik, before his death, commanded that Chonyo his second son should serve in his place. Shimi his brother, who was two and a half years older than he, became jealous of him. Shimi said to him: “Come, I will teach you the order of the service.” He dressed him in a woman’s tunic (unkali) and girded him with her ribbon (tziltzol) and stood him by the altar, and Shimi said to his brother Kohanim: “See what this one vowed to his beloved and fulfilled …” The Kohanim wanted to kill him, and he fled to Alexandria in Egypt and built an altar there — the words of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehudah relates that the incident was that Chonyo did not accept it, and nonetheless Chonyo became jealous, etc.

In Josephus’s Jewish Antiquities it is related that Shimon HaTzaddik left a small son named Chonyo, and Elazar, Shimon’s brother, served in his place. Hyman identifies the Chonyo who built an altar in Egypt as the son of Shimon ben Chonyo ben Shimon HaTzaddik; Hyman therefore insists that the Gemara means Shimon, the grandson of Shimon HaTzaddik, and the name “HaTzaddik” became corrupted from the preceding story.
Hyman has already treated this at length in the entry Shimon HaTzaddik.

notes.text: Saved Davidson English Menachot109b describes the woman’s tunic/ribbon disguise and explicitly makes Chonyo jealous in Yehudah’s alternative version. Hyman’s Josephus comparison, grandson reconstruction and claim that HaTzaddik migrated from a prior story remain attributed, not independently verified print history.

The inspected Davidson Menachot 109b gives two alternative jealousy accounts: Shimi in Meir’s version and Chonyo in Yehudah’s version, with different accounts of the Egyptian altar. Hyman’s Josephus comparison, grandson reconstruction and proposed migration of HaTzaddik from the preceding story remain his historical argument; those exact Josephus and printing claims were not independently inspected.
